passages.happening:
In that day the rescued will say, ‘O LORD, I will praise You’ (verse 1). Although God was angry, ‘Your anger has turned away, and You have comforted me’ (verse 1).

‘Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and not be afraid. For the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and He also has become my salvation’ (verse 2).

‘With joy you will draw water from the springs of salvation’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 1 to 12 form the first large movement of Isaiah. They open with a courtroom charge against Judah and pass through the prophet's call, the crisis of King Ahaz, the promised child, the fall of Assyria and the Spirit-filled king. After so much judgment, the section ends not with a warning but with a hymn.

The song borrows its central line from Israel's oldest story of rescue. When Israel crossed the sea out of Egypt, Moses and the people sang that the LORD was their strength and song and had become their salvation. Chapter 11 had just promised a second exodus with a highway home. Chapter 12 gives the people the song for it.

Water in the dry hill country of Judah was never taken for granted. Jerusalem depended on the Gihon spring outside its walls and on cisterns cut in the rock. Drawing water was daily work. To speak of drawing water from the springs of salvation turns an ordinary chore into a picture of joy that never runs dry. Later Jewish practice tied verse 3 to the Feast of Tabernacles, when priests drew water from the Pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar.

Some scholars think this closing hymn was added when the first section of the book was arranged, because it gathers phrases from the Psalms and Exodus as worship songs do. Others see no reason it could not come from Isaiah, who writes psalm-like poetry elsewhere.
passages.later: The line comes from the song at the sea: ‘The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation’ (Exodus 15:2), sung again in a psalm (Psalm 118:14).
passages.asks: The singer remembers God's anger and rejoices that it has turned away. Ask whether you have known both, and whether you can sing about the second without forgetting the first. And ask where you go each day to draw water, and whether it is from the springs of salvation.

passages.t: Make his works known among the peoples
passages.happening:
On that day they will say, “Give praise to the LORD; proclaim His name! Make His works known among the peoples; declare that His name is exalted.” (verse 4).

‘Sing to the LORD, for He has done glorious things. Let this be known in all the earth’ (verse 5).

‘Cry out and sing, O citizen of Zion, for great among you is the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The single voice of verses 1 and 2 becomes a whole community. The calls to praise, proclaim and sing are the language of temple worship, where the congregation gave thanks aloud and told of God's deeds.

The song looks outward. God's works are to be made known among the peoples and in all the earth. The next section of the book, beginning in chapter 13, turns to the nations, and this song has already prepared for it.

The last line ends where the book's vision of God began, in chapter 6: the Holy One of Israel. The holiness that made Isaiah cry out that he was ruined is now in the middle of the city, and the people shout for joy.
passages.later: A psalm sings the same call: ‘Give thanks to the LORD, call upon His name; make known His deeds among the nations’ (Psalm 105:1).
passages.asks: The rescued people are told to make God's works known among the peoples. Ask what God has done for you that you have kept to yourself. And ask what it would mean for the Holy One to be great in the middle of your ordinary life.
